I'm an avid backer in the Design category, with over a dozen backed projects under my belt. Most everything I've backed has either successfully come to life, or is still on track to completion. I admit I too have one video game that's taken around a year now, but I backed it minimally and I enjoy their updates, so I'm not too worried about it.

As for how I don't have a dozen failures and a couple hundred down the toilet, I can tell you this is because I'm very discerning about what I do back and from whom. If you're curious on how to Kickstarter better, here's what I look for:

Who is making it? Second time campaigners are great. So are engineers. So are those with a lot of passion for their work. Then, what is the project? Do they have a prototype? If so, does it work, and demonstrate the complete functionality of the end product? Then, does the person/people appear to have the skills required to get it done, and possibly most importantly, does the project look feasible? Finally, how are they doing it? If they're just making T-shirts, there's nothing special there, that infrastructure exists already. Same with things that are getting CNC'd or laser cut. All they need to do is buy some factory time, and boom, they ship it. However, if it comes out of a mold, it's going to need to get tooled, which is often sticky because it tends to cost more money than backers or first time creators think, and where bankruptcy tends to happen. If it needs tooling, and tooling is complete, it's a really, really good sign. Maybe I should make this a flow chart.

Anyway, a good example of the kind of project I avoid was that group of people who "liked to play laser tag", behind iTager, a group who were "going to revolutionize laser tag". This was a project I figured would have problems, (the whole mounting on firearms thing aside) that later got cancelled. https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/itager/itager

Problems:

  • They didn't demonstrate much knowledge about the electronics they were making (no one of product design or engineering background)
  • They didn't have concrete plans for its design
  • They didn't have a convincing prototype (though they claimed it was ready, they didn't demo in any effective way)

I hope that helped. Feel free to respond in the comments.

Regards,

Don't keep more than 6 months of emergency money in a savings account. Of course you should save more than that but keep the remainder of your savings in investment assets. You lose money in the long run by keeping it in a savings account. Only reason to have one is liquidity.

Also, the more you've got saved up in investment accounts, the less you need in liquid cash. If you've got enough money to live for year or two sitting in an "emergency" investment fund you can get by with having a month or so in cash.
The concern is that you might need to take it out at a loss. If the market is down when, say, your car has engine trouble you're going to wish you had it liquid.

Your car is going to have engine trouble and you should just save some money for when that happens. Likewise, you're going to need new clothes, computers, etc. and you ideally you want to have a budget that lets you set aside money for these things. They're not emergencies because you can count on them occurring. With proper planning, you shouldn't have to hit your emergency fund for expected expenses.

You should always keep some cash available so that "minor" emergencies can be covered without selling stocks or whatever. As long as you're only hitting the investment fund for large problems (like covering for a period of unemployment, major medical expenses, etc.) you should be okay just having enough in your cash based emergency fund to get you through a month or so. For the invested emergency fund, even though you might have to sell on a down turn, chances are much better that you'll be selling on an upturn relative to holding the same money in a savings account. On average the stock market as a whole will have grown and, since you're only hitting that fund for big unexpected things, there should be enough time between sell-offs that that averaging should work in your favor. Of course, invested emergency funds should be tied to something relatively stable like large index funds and never used to buy individual stocks or bonds.

Note that you don't want to start your emergency fund by investing it in the stock market. When I did mine, I built out 6 months worth of cash. From then on, for every extra month's worth I saved I put that month plus one from the cash fund into the stock market until I had one month in cash and 11 months in index funds (like below).

Month's worth of cash months in savings/cash months in index funds
1 1 0
2 2 0
3 3 0
4 4 0
5 5 0
6 6 0
7 5 2
8 4 4
9 3 6
10 2 8
11 1 10
12 1 11

As a worst case scenario, I expect to be able to sell my 11 months worth of stock for 5-6 months worth of cash. It's true that I would lose a lot of money if that happened (sort of), but the chances are better that I'd sell it for more than 11 months worth of cash.

The American system of politics is very difficult to describe in some ways. It is an always-wobbling, EXTREMELY complicated balance between citizens (both as a whole and as many, many, often overlapping subgroups and special interests), business interests, and government itself. The problem is that the public has a strong sense of apathy, or feels helpless. The former is difficult to shake them from (especially when we have, say, anti-intellectualism running through society), and the latter is a self-fulfilling prophecy.

Over time, the tremendous wealth that the US has built up, particularly since World War II, has bought the luxury of indifference while still remaining relatively free and fed. This is now eroding. Fast. It's been eroding for quite some time but it has begun to accelerate, with TPP acting as a major step in that direction. And the question is, will the public pick up the slack and get involved? Good question. I believe that someone once asked Thomas Jefferson precisely what he and the other Founding Fathers had given them. His reply was, "A democracy... if you can keep it." That is the question - can we? And it is a question that will be asked eternally until the US as we know it is no more.

With things like TPP being seriously considered, while it isn't too late, it also isn't looking very good. That said, despite the stubborn refusal of the media to cover it, despite reddit censoring it off the front page, stories are creeping in and information is getting out. SOPA didn't get a lot of coverage, either, until it was forced. Defeating it is still possible.
